Hi [~accountid:63a2bfff48b367d78a14db98] sorry that this took more time than expected, but thank you for creating a ticket and your patience. 

I have made some research, and wrote down my conclusion below.  

Whether it's legal for a Merchant like Bolt to charge a customer the original full price after a discounted subscription payment fails during a grace period can depend on several factors including the terms and conditions of the subscription agreement, local consumer protection laws, and potentially other local regulations of each market.

In my point of view, these are the main aspects we should consider: 

# Terms and Conditions/internal policies: Review the terms and conditions of the subscription agreement you agreed to when signing up for the service. This document should outline the company's policies regarding payments, discounts, late fees, and grace periods. Bolt Plus Terms and Conditions govern how we handle situations like failed payments and grace periods. 

# Consumer Protection Laws and industry regulations: Many countries have consumer protection laws that regulate business practices and ensure fairness in transactions. These laws may impose restrictions on how companies can handle subscription payments, including late fees and price changes. However, considering we have covered the scenario of you questions in our T&Cs, I am confident to believe we have validated that the T&Cs are aligned with consumer laws (at least in the markets where Bolt Plus is available) or, if there is no validation, we have taken a risk based approach within our appetite.  

# Good Faith and Fair Dealing: In many jurisdictions, there's an implied duty of good faith and fair dealing in contracts. This means that both parties are expected to act honestly and fairly in their dealings with each other. If the company's actions are deemed to be unfair or deceptive, it could be challenged legally. 

In conclusion, to answer your questions:

* What price should customer pay during the grace period? 

This depends on what our [Bolt Plus Terms and Conditions |https://bolt.eu/en/legal/bolt-plus/?category=rides]say together with the specific campaign (discount) special terms (if any). If we have offered a discount, and the special terms do not regulate what happens if the discounted payment fails, the general Bolt Plus Terms apply. 


Bolt Plus terms cover benefits intended to promote usage of Bolt Plus subscription and Bolt’s platform (collectively called “*Benefits*”).  

Then, Bolt has the right to cancel the subscription. See 2. Duration and Charges: 
_”Please note that in case your payment methods available in the Bolt App are declined or payments fail in other ways,_ *_Bolt is authorised to cancel your Bolt Plus subscription and your Benefits will expire at the end of a billing cycle._*_”_  

Note that Bolt Plus terms allow Bolt to charge any payment method associated with the customer Bolt account in case the customer primary payment method is declined or no longer available to Bolt for payment of the Subscription Fee. 

Then, if we have offered a discount, the payment failed, the price of the subscription should be discounted until they expire at the end of a billing cycle. 

Same clause 2 says “In case offered Benefits significantly change and/or Subscription Fee increases - we will notify you about this in advance of the next auto-renewal.“

”Billing cycle” is not defined. What is this cycle? 

* Is there any limitations and requirements to not use the original discounted price there (preferable way for us)?

Did I understand correctly that we prefer to charge the full price if the customer failed to pay the discounted price on time?

The only limitations are those in our T&Cs. Meaning that Bolt can cancel your Bolt Plus subscription and your Benefits at the end of a billing cycle. 

Ps. Note that a consumer can always complain about anything, so it is very important than these things are clearly communicated to them according to Bolt Plus Terms.

If you have any questions, let me know I’m happy to have a talk about this.

Another use case: combining pre-aggregated and fact data in Looker

The way I imagine this could be possible:

* create a data mart, for example city + hour + metric1
* create a view in spark+presto with fact table level of detail and the automatically generated metric query defining the metric1 column
* define data mart as view in looker with metric1 as measure
* define the view in looker as a view with metric1 as measure
* define an explore that dynamically picks between the data mart view and the view view

→ user can select any level of detail. if they select something pre-calculated, they get fast results from the data mart. if they select something not pre-calculated, they get slow results from the view.

The longer text with references to legal texts can be found here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hkifTbdsjYamkJdePqTdeEZA1nfmqIvbOBFoO-DUHWI/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hkifTbdsjYamkJdePqTdeEZA1nfmqIvbOBFoO-DUHWI/edit?usp=sharing]

The short answer is that it should be OK to roll out this feature in Finland. The requirement to show the trip price to Riders has already been completed by the time when additional stops are added.

Via the T&C and the app the Riders are provided with the following information:

* the initial price is an estimation;
* the basis for determining the final price;
* the price may change upon certain conditions (such as a longer trip or surcharges in the form of a waiting fee).

When confirming the order, Riders give their express consent for the possibility of a price change and also for the possibility of surcharges. Riders give an additional consent for adding the new stop which can result in price changes.

Provided that the above conditions are met, the Finnish laws do not require the Riders to be informed of the changed price when additional stops are added at their request. Therefore, assuming that the Finnish consumer protection authority interprets the laws the same way, it is OK to roll out this feature in Finland.

I looked at the timeframe from *2022-07* till *2024-02* (20 complete months), for the UK and London. The data for calculations comes from two sources, *Driver Data Hourly* and *Global Event Assessment Tool* (driver consequential blocks marked in the tool).

For accessing the impact on GMV I use an estimate of lost earnings per month, which is based on the data about Drivers' Earnings per Hour and Average Online Hours.

The overview is broken down into three parts:

* *Consequential Blocks* _(1-Day, 3-Day, 7-Day, 28-Day Blocks)_
* *Hard-Blocks* _(excluding Customer Safety Support Block)_
* *Combined* 

For each month, there is a *Total Lost Earnings* value and its *Percentage of GMV*. 
Additionally, you can find a month-over-month *Percentage Change*, where the declining trend is highlighted in {color:#36b37e}*green*{color}. 

It’s not very obvious how to estimate the effect of Hard-Blocks on GMV since I believe it has a cumulative effect on all the months to come. But it should still be a good basis for comparison.
